idiom_name: scala.util.Using (Using.resource / Using.apply / Using.Manager) over AutoCloseable or a Using.Releasable
implementation_notes: scala.util.Using is the library realization: Using.resource(acquire) { r => ... } releases on every exit path, Using.apply wraps the result in Try, and Using.Manager tracks several resources registered at construction (including resources acquired inside a constructor). The release step is the customization seam - a Using.Releasable, or plain AutoCloseable, decides whether close hands the resource back to its owner - so a lending API should return a type whose close performs the hand-back or expose its own releaser. The classic C++ structure is replaced by Using plus a releaser; effect systems express the same hand-back as a first-class acquire/release pair.
code_sketch:
Using.resource(pool.checkout()) { conn =>   // released on all exit paths
  handle(conn)
}                                           // close() => returned to the pool

Using.Manager { use =>                      // several borrowed resources
  val a = use(pool.checkout())
  handle(a)
}
pitfalls: Using combines failures but discards non-suppressible or ControlThrowable exceptions, so a failed hand-back can vanish from the failure chain - keep release non-throwing where possible.
A Releasable that calls the wrong path (a generic close on a pooled object) either destroys a borrowed resource or leaks its slot; the releaser is the single place to get right.
Using holds the resource only for the block; returning it from the block or letting it escape into a Future uses an already-released resource - Scala will not stop you.
